readerTitle: Why your tenth improvement is worth less than your first
caseNote: 가상 사례 (출퇴근길, 회계 사무소, 식품 유통 창고) · 모든 수치는 설명용. S-커브 개념은 Richard Foster(1986)가 대중화
insight: 개선 한 번에 드는 비용은 늘고 얻는 효과가 줄어든다면, 노력이 부족한 것이 아니라 방식 자체가 한계에 다가가고 있다는 신호다. 그때가 다음 방식에 작게 투자할 때다.
misconception: 지금 방식을 더 열심히 다듬으면 계속 나아진다. 새 방식이 지금 더 못하면 신경 쓸 필요가 없다.

sources.text: Foster, R. N. (1986). Innovation: The Attacker's Advantage. Summit Books.

factChecks.note: Richard Foster가 McKinsey 컨설턴트로서 1986년 저서 'Innovation: The Attacker's Advantage'에서 기술 S-커브 개념을 대중화했다는 내용을 게시 전 확인하세요.
회계 사무소 계산: 10일 − 4일(1~2년차) − 2일(3~4년차) − 0.2일(5년차) = 3.8일. 2번 카드의 '10일에서 4일, 올해 3.8일'과 일치합니다.
'유망한 신기술이 수년간 기존 방식보다 못했다'는 일반적 서술이며 특정 사례나 수치를 들지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why your tenth improvement is worth less than your first
body: The first time you rethought your commute, you saved 15 minutes with a new route and an earlier train. The next tweak saved five. Now each new idea saves a few seconds.
Your commute didn't stop improving because you stopped trying. It stopped because the method, driving that road, has a limit. Businesses hit the same wall, and most don't notice.

image.label: A commuter's watch showing shrinking time savings
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 출근길 위에 시계 세 개가 놓여 있고, 각각 '−15 min', '−5 min', '−10 sec' 라벨. 시계가 점점 작아지는 연출. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your best process is barely getting better.
body: You run a bookkeeping firm. Over five years, checklists, templates and training cut your clients' month-end close from 10 days to 4. This year, a full round of training cut it to 3.8.
Meanwhile, software that reads receipts and bank statements automatically makes more errors than your staff today. But it gets better every year. What do you do?

options.text: Invest more in training and checklists. It's proven
options.feedback: Safe and familiar, but each hour saved now costs more, and the ceiling is how fast people can key in and check numbers.

options.text: Keep the current process, and put a small team on the software with a few clients
options.feedback: You keep today's income while learning the new method before it overtakes the old. It costs some money and attention now.

options.text: Move every client to the software now
options.feedback: You'd be early to the new method, but today it's worse. Clients would feel the errors long before it catches up.

cards.title: Same effort, shrinking gains.

breakdown.label: Year 5
breakdown.detail: A full training round, at a higher cost

cards.callout: Each step cost more and gave back less. The process wasn't broken. It was close to its natural limit.

cards.title: The S-curve
body: An **S-curve** shows how a method improves as you put effort into it. Early on, progress is slow while people figure it out. Then it speeds up as the key ideas click. Finally it flattens as the method nears a limit built into it.
Plot effort against results and you get a stretched letter S. The bookkeeping firm is near the top of its curve.

image.label: One S-shaped curve with three phases labeled
image.brief: 가로축 'Effort', 세로축 'Performance'인 S자 곡선 하나. 구간별로 'Slow start', 'Fast climb', 'Flattening' 라벨. 위쪽에 점선으로 'Built-in limit' 표시.

cards.title: The new curve starts lower, and ends higher.
body: A new method begins on its own S-curve, usually below the old one. Early receipt-reading software was worse than a careful clerk. That's why it's easy to dismiss.
But its ceiling is higher. If it climbs fast enough, it crosses the old curve. Firms that wait for the crossing start at the bottom while rivals are already in the steep part.
Richard Foster, a McKinsey consultant, made this idea popular in his 1986 book *Innovation: The Attacker's Advantage*.

image.label: Two S-curves, the new one crossing the old
image.brief: S자 곡선 두 개. 회색 'Old method' 곡선은 일찍 평평해지고, 파란 'New method' 곡선은 낮게 시작해 가파르게 올라가 교차. 교차점에 'Crossover' 라벨.

cards.title: It's not just technology.
body: S-curves appear wherever a method has a ceiling: a sales channel, a store format, a delivery route, a marketing message. Your first trade show brings a flood of leads. Your fifth brings a trickle.
The signal is the same each time: **more spend for less gain**, and a limit set by the method itself, not by how hard you try.
cards.softwareNote: Growth channels follow S-curves too. Paid ads may bring cheap users early, then cost more per user as you reach the edge of the audience. Strong teams test the next channel before the current one flattens.

cards.title: A flat stretch isn't always the top.
body: Sometimes a curve stalls, then climbs again after a breakthrough. Sometimes the new method never catches up. Many promising technologies stayed worse than the old way for years.
Jump too early and you lose money and customers. Jump too late and you start behind. The usual answer is **small, cheap bets** on the new curve while the old one still pays the bills.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You manage a regional grocery distributor. Pickers walk the aisles filling orders for local stores. Accuracy and speed have improved every year.
Which sign best suggests your picking method is near the top of its S-curve?

options.text: Order volume grew more slowly this quarter
options.feedback: Worth watching, but slower volume often reflects demand, not the limits of your method. It tells you little about the picking itself.

options.text: Each improvement costs more and gains less, and the limit is how fast a person can walk the aisles
options.feedback: That's the S-curve signal: shrinking returns plus a ceiling built into the method. Time to pilot a new layout or scanning in one zone.

options.text: A competitor announced it is buying picking robots
options.feedback: A rival's move can push you into a costly jump before the new method suits you. Look at your own curve first.

cards.title: Every method has a ceiling. Watch for it.
body: When each improvement costs more and gives less, you may be near the top of your S-curve. Start small on the next method while the current one still pays.
**Try it today:** pick one process you've improved for years. Write down your last three improvements, what each cost and what each gained. Is the gain shrinking?
